q: During a real, publicly reported outage at a payroll vendor, a caller tells a credit union clerk that he is on the vendor's incident team. He quotes the correct outage ticket number from the vendor's status page and asks her to read back the MFA code that just arrived 'to resync the account.' The clerk later asks the security team what made the call so convincing. Which technique BEST answers her question?
w: The believable story built on a real event, the pretext, is what made the request seem legitimate. Vishing is the channel (a phone call) and impersonation is the role the caller played, but neither explains the credibility, and no text message was involved, so it isn't smishing.
h: Vishing is the phone. Pretexting is the script read into the phone.

q: An email to a manufacturer's accounts payable team appears to come from the CEO. It mentions an acquisition announced in yesterday's press release and asks for an urgent wire to a 'closing escrow account.' In the post-incident review, the CFO asks which technique made the request seem legitimate, rather than how it was delivered. Which answer BEST fits that question?
w: Tying the request to real news creates a believable pretext, which is what made it seem legitimate. Phishing is the delivery method, BEC would require a real, compromised mailbox (none is described), and brand impersonation means posing as a company's brand, not an executive.
h: Ask 'why did they believe it?', not 'how did it arrive?'

q: Users are repeatedly disconnected, then reconnect to a network with the SAME SSID and a stronger signal that shows a login page. The wireless IDS logs a flood of deauthentication frames. What is this?
w: Same SSID plus stronger signal plus forced deauth is the detail that only fits an evil twin.
h: A rogue AP is a stranger in the building. An evil twin is a stranger wearing your coworker's face.

ack: The correct option is the fixed term name '802.11w Protected Management Frames'.
q: Attackers at a hotel conference center repeatedly send spoofed deauthentication frames to knock attendees off the event Wi-Fi, then lure them onto a look-alike access point. The venue's APs support WPA3. Which control BEST stops the forged frames themselves?
o: Hiding the SSID from beacon broadcasts
MAC address filtering on every AP
w: PMF (mandatory with WPA3) cryptographically protects management frames, so clients ignore forged deauthentication frames. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filtering are trivially bypassed and don't authenticate frames, and WPS affects PIN-based enrollment, not deauthentication.
h: PMF signs the 'you're disconnected' notes.

q: A 15-person accounting office with no IT staff wants firewall, gateway antivirus, URL filtering, and site-to-site VPN in one box, managed from one console at a low fixed cost. Which is BEST?
w: Small office + all-in-one + single console + low cost is the UTM tell.
h: UTM is the Swiss Army knife for a small shop. NGFW is the specialist's scalpel.

q: A fintech's security policy says 'data in transit must be protected.' A second document, also approved by the CISO, says 'all external web services must use TLS 1.2 or higher with AES-GCM cipher suites; exceptions require CISO approval.' An auditor asks how the second document should be classified in the governance hierarchy. Which classification is correct?
w: Specific, mandatory technical requirements (named protocol versions and ciphers) that support a policy make a standard. The policy is the first document, a procedure would give steps, and a guideline would be optional.
h: Policy = purpose. Standard = specifics.

q: An insurer's security team publishes a document for employees. It says staff 'should consider' a password manager for personal accounts and lists three reputable options. Employees who don't follow it face no consequences. In the document hierarchy, which type is this?
w: 'Should consider', with no consequences, is a recommendation, which makes it a guideline. Standards and policies are mandatory, and procedures give required steps.
h: Guideline = good idea, optional.

q: User jlee lives and works in Phoenix. The VPN report below covers one Tuesday, and jlee says he worked from home all day on his laptop. Which indicator does the report show?
c:
user=jlee  src=68.2.14.9   (Phoenix, AZ)  start=09:00  end=12:00  device=CORP-LT-118
user=jlee  src=98.167.3.40 (Tempe, AZ)    start=10:30  end=11:15  device=unknown
w: The two sessions overlap in time from different devices, so two parties are using one account. Phoenix and Tempe are next to each other, so it isn't impossible travel; logging timing and inaccessible resources aren't involved.
h: Check the clocks before the map.

q: A logged-in banking customer reads a forum in another tab. A post contains a 1×1 image whose src is https://bank.example.com/transfer?to=88213409&amount=4900, and the money moves. What attack is this?
w: No script runs — the victim's browser is tricked into sending a request and attaches the bank's cookie automatically.
h: CSRF is a forged signature: the attacker writes the check, your browser signs it with your cookie.

q: Customers of an online bank lost money when a forum post embedded a hidden image whose URL triggered a funds transfer. Their browsers attached valid bank session cookies automatically. The bank cannot control the forum. Which fix on the bank's side BEST prevents this?
o: Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite settings on the bank's site
A content security policy deployed on all of the forum's pages
The HttpOnly flag on the bank's session cookie
Input validation on the forum's post field
w: This is CSRF; unpredictable tokens and SameSite cookies stop forged cross-site requests from succeeding. The bank can't change the forum's CSP or input handling, and HttpOnly stops script from reading cookies but doesn't stop the browser from sending them.
h: You don't stop forged checks by asking the forger's print shop to behave.

q: Stored XSS on a portal lets a script read the session cookie and send it out. The code fix will take weeks. The cookie is currently: Set-Cookie: SID=7f3c; Secure; SameSite=Lax. Which change BEST reduces impact now?
o: Scope Domain to the portal host only
w: The attack is script reading document.cookie — only HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript.
h: HttpOnly Hides it from script (anti-XSS). SameSite = Stay on this Site (anti-CSRF).

q: A cloud-hosted marketplace lets sellers import product images from a URL. A WAF log shows the request below, and the response contained JSON with an access key instead of image data. Which attack occurred?
w: The server was tricked into fetching an internal-only address, the cloud metadata service, and returned what it got. Traversal reads files with ../, command injection runs OS commands, and reflected XSS runs script in a victim's browser.
h: 169.254.169.254 in a URL field means SSRF going after cloud keys.

q: After an SSRF incident, a startup's cloud team must stop any future SSRF bug in its image importer from reaching the instance metadata service and returning credentials. The importer legitimately fetches only from three partner CDNs. Which pair of controls BEST meets this?
o: Require IMDSv2 and allow-list approved fetch destinations
Add HttpOnly and Secure attributes to every session cookie
Enable full-disk encryption on the importer instances
Deploy anti-CSRF tokens on every importer form
w: IMDSv2 requires a session token that a simple SSRF request can't obtain, and an allow-list limits fetches to known destinations. Cookie flags, disk encryption, and CSRF tokens don't stop the server from requesting internal URLs.
h: Don't let the server deliver to addresses inside your own building.

q: What happens to traffic from 10.5.5.5 to 172.16.40.20 on TCP 443?
c:
#  Action  Proto  Source  Destination      Port
1  PERMIT  TCP    any     172.16.40.0/24   443
2  DENY    TCP    any     172.16.40.20     443
3  DENY    IP     any     any              any (log)
w: 172.16.40.20 is inside 172.16.40.0/24, so rule 1 matches first and processing stops; rule 2 is shadowed.
h: The bouncer stops reading at the first line that mentions you.

q: Using the same rules, what is the BEST fix so 172.16.40.20 is blocked on 443 while the rest of 172.16.40.0/24 still accepts HTTPS from anywhere?
c:
1  PERMIT  TCP  any  172.16.40.0/24  443
2  DENY    TCP  any  172.16.40.20    443
3  DENY    IP   any  any             any (log)
o: Change rule 1's source to the internal subnet only
w: Specific before broad; the other options break the "other servers from anywhere" requirement or open everything.
h: A fix that solves one requirement by breaking another is always wrong.

q: While cleaning up a branch firewall, an administrator deletes the final rule shown below, assuming it was redundant. Traffic that matches none of the remaining rules then arrives. What happens to that traffic?
c:
10  PERMIT  TCP  10.8.0.0/16  any  443
20  PERMIT  UDP  10.8.0.0/16  10.0.0.53  53
30  DENY    IP   any          any  any   (log)   <- deleted
o: Still blocked by the implicit deny, but no longer logged
It's allowed, because no rule now denies it
It's blocked and logged exactly as before
The firewall fails open until another deny rule is re-added
w: Firewalls end with an implicit deny, so unmatched traffic is still blocked; the explicit rule existed mainly to log those denials. Nothing becomes allowed, logging is lost, and deleting a rule doesn't change the device's failure mode.
h: Not on the list? Still not getting in, but nobody writes it down.

q: A hospital's SOC wants complete visibility of traffic crossing the core switch. Clinical leadership insists the change must add no latency and must not create a new device that could take the network down if it fails. Which device and placement BEST meet both requirements?
o: An IDS fed by a tap or SPAN port
An IPS placed inline at the core uplink
A WAF placed in front of the core switch
NAC enforcement on the core uplink ports
w: An IDS on a copy of the traffic adds no latency and can't interrupt flows if it fails, though it can only alert. An inline IPS sits in the traffic path, a WAF protects web applications, and NAC controls device admission.
h: Watching a copy can't break the original.

q: Red team tests show exploit traffic passing between a manufacturer's internal firewall and its core switch. The CISO requires that such traffic be stopped automatically as it happens, and operations has accepted the small added latency. Which device and placement fit?
o: An IPS placed inline on that link
An IDS attached to a SPAN port on the core
An IDS fed by a passive network tap
A SIEM correlation rule with email alerting
w: Only a device in the traffic path can block packets in real time. IDS sensors on SPAN ports or taps see copies and can only alert, and a SIEM rule alerts after the logs arrive.
h: To stop traffic, you have to stand in its way.

q: A retailer is deploying a WAF to protect three public web servers in its DMZ. The perimeter firewall already drops non-HTTPS traffic. The architect must pick where the WAF goes so it inspects all web traffic before any server receives it, while staying protected itself. Where should it be placed?
o: In the DMZ, behind the firewall, before the servers
Outside the perimeter firewall, facing the internet
Between the web servers and the database tier only
On each customer's workstation as a browser plug-in
w: Behind the firewall and in front of the web tier, the WAF inspects every web request while the firewall shields it. Outside the firewall it's exposed to all internet noise, between the web and database tiers it misses attacks on the web servers, and customers' machines aren't yours to control.
h: The firewall sweeps the street; the WAF checks guests at the door.

q: A ticketing site runs three web servers behind a load balancer. Each user's cart and login state live only in the memory of whichever server first handled them, and rewriting the app isn't possible this year. Users complain about being logged out and losing carts mid-purchase. Which load balancer setting BEST fixes this?
o: Least connections with no session affinity
w: Sticky sessions keep each user on the server that holds their state. Round-robin and least connections without affinity move users between servers, and active/passive would waste two servers without addressing session state.
h: Keep the same bank teller, because only that teller has your paperwork.

q: A clinic's NAC uses 802.1X plus a posture check. A staff laptop authenticates successfully but is missing three critical patches, so it fails posture. The clinic wants it fixed quickly without letting it reach clinical systems. What should NAC do?
o: Quarantine VLAN with access only to patch servers
Shut down the switch port until IT re-enables it
Grant full access and send an alert to the SOC
Disable the user's Active Directory account
w: A remediation VLAN lets the device reach update servers but nothing sensitive, then admits it once it's patched. Disabling the port creates help desk work without fixing the laptop, full access defeats posture checking, and the user did nothing wrong.
h: NAC quarantine is urgent care: not sent home, not let into surgery.

q: A hospital installs an inline IPS in front of its clinical systems. The chief medical officer states that patient care must never stop because of a security appliance failure, and the CISO accepts that uninspected traffic is the lesser risk during an outage. Which failure mode should the IPS use?
w: Fail-open passes traffic uninspected if the IPS fails, putting availability first as leadership requires. Fail-closed (and the deny-on-failure variants) would stop clinical traffic.
h: Open door: traffic keeps flowing. Closed door: everything stops.

q: At 02:31, right after 4.8 GB leaves the network, EDR shows: vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet. What is the attacker MOST likely doing?
c:
02:05  Event ID 4672  svc_backup  special privileges assigned
02:18  rclone.exe  outbound 4.8 GB -> 185.220.101.47
02:31  vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet
w: Deleting shadow copies removes easy restores; privileges were already gained at 4672.
h: Cutting the phone line before kicking in the door — encryption is minutes away.

q: At 02:33, responders confirm that an attacker has a foothold on workstation WS-HR-112, has stolen the svc_backup service account's credentials, and is staging data on file server FS-02. Encryption usually follows within minutes. Legal wants memory evidence preserved. What is the BEST containment step?
o: Isolate both hosts with EDR and disable the compromised account
Block the attacker's external IP address and keep monitoring closely
Power off every server in the data center at once
Reimage WS-HR-112 from the gold image right away
w: Containment has to cover every foothold, both hosts and the stolen credential, while keeping the machines running for memory capture. Blocking one IP leaves the account and hosts in the attacker's hands, a mass power-off destroys evidence and disrupts everything, and reimaging is eradication that also destroys evidence.
h: Lock every room the burglar is in and take back the key.

q: After a ransomware incident in which attackers brute-forced the svc_backup account from a workstation, the identity team must harden it. The account runs scheduled backup jobs on one backup server and never logs on interactively. Which change is BEST?
o: Limit where it can log on and use an auto-rotated gMSA password
Lock the account after five failed attempts
Require SMS-based MFA whenever the service account authenticates
Rename the account to something less obvious
w: Limiting where the account can log on and letting the system rotate a long password removes both the reuse and guessing paths. Lockout invites a denial of service against backups, SMS MFA can't work for non-interactive jobs, and renaming is obscurity.
h: A service account should open one door, with a key that changes itself.

q: Attackers use a reverse-proxy kit (AiTM) that relays logins to the real portal in real time and steals the session cookie. Which MFA BEST stops this even if the admin is fooled?
w: FIDO2 signs a challenge bound to the real domain, so the fake site gets nothing usable.
h: Codes are passwords you say out loud. A FIDO2 key only fits your bank's actual lock.

q: An engineering firm's attackers have stolen passwords and are now spamming push approval requests at night, hoping a sleepy user taps Approve. The firm is considering push notifications with number matching. Against which attack is that feature MOST effective?
w: Number matching forces the user to enter a code shown on the real login screen, which stops blind approvals of spammed prompts. A user actively logging in to an AiTM proxy still sees and enters the real number, SIM swapping targets SMS, and pass-the-hash doesn't involve MFA prompts.
h: Number matching stops 'approve, approve, approve', not a user who's been fooled.

q: A hospital is deploying Wi-Fi for clinical tablets. Requirements: certificates on both the server and every device, no passwords anywhere in the exchange, and the ability to revoke any single tablet. Which EAP method meets all three?
w: EAP-TLS uses mutual certificate authentication, so each device certificate can be revoked individually and no password is used. PEAP and EAP-TTLS normally carry passwords inside a server-authenticated tunnel, and EAP-FAST uses protected access credentials instead of device certificates.
h: EAP-TLS: two certificates, server and client.

q: A law firm's staff join the corporate Wi-Fi by typing their existing Active Directory usernames and passwords. A packet capture shows that only the RADIUS server presents a certificate, and the password travels inside an encrypted tunnel. Which EAP method is the firm MOST likely using?
w: PEAP builds a TLS tunnel using only the server's certificate and passes MSCHAPv2 credentials inside it. EAP-TLS needs client certificates, EAP-FAST uses PACs, and EAP-MD5 offers no tunnel and is weak.
h: PEAP: one certificate, then a password through the tunnel.

q: A VPN portal certificate is valid, publicly trusted, has a matching wildcard SAN and RSA 3072 — but every client rejects it. What's wrong?
o: It isn't authorized for Server Authentication
The wildcard can't cover a VPN hostname
RSA 3072 is too weak for TLS
It needs the Client Authentication EKU instead
w: A TLS server certificate needs the Server Authentication EKU (…3.1); code signing can't do that job.
h: EKU is the job title on the badge. A valid "Code Signing" badge can't open the server room.

q: A company's new certificate has the SAN entry *.corp.example.com. Before deployment, the PKI team checks which internal hostnames it will cover. Which hostname will FAIL name validation?
ack: Options are hostnames; the item tests one-label wildcard matching.
w: A wildcard matches exactly one label in place of the asterisk, so a name two labels deep doesn't match. The other three each sit one label below corp.example.com.
h: The asterisk is one seat at the table, not the whole row.

q: A medication database must be recoverable to any specific minute in the last 24 hours. Last year a bad script's corruption copied to the standby replica instantly. Nightly full backups exist. What should be added?
o: Synchronous replication to a second site
w: Restore the nightly full, then replay the journal to one minute before the bad change; replication copies the damage.
h: Replication is a mirror — it shows the coffee stain too. Journaling is a video you can rewind.

q: The BIA sets an RTO of 4 hours for the core system. Measured MTTR is 12 hours and MTBF is 18 months. What is the conclusion?
o: The RTO can't be met; a standby system or faster SLA is needed
The RTO is met because failures are rare
MTBF offsets the MTTR, so no change is needed
w: Compare the measured average (MTTR) to the target (RTO); how rarely it fails never makes repairs faster.
h: RTO is the deadline. MTTR is how long your homework actually takes.

q: A coding-challenge website runs code submitted by strangers on its own servers. Last month, a Linux kernel flaw let processes break out of container isolation, and the operators expect more such flaws. Modest overhead per submission is acceptable. Which isolation approach is BEST?
o: Run each one in its own virtual machine
Containers with a read-only root file system
Microservices separated behind an API gateway
Containers with stricter cgroup resource limits
w: Each VM has its own kernel, isolated by the hypervisor, so a kernel exploit in one doesn't reach the others. Read-only file systems and cgroup limits still share the host kernel, and an API gateway manages traffic rather than isolating code.
h: Untrusted code gets its own kernel.

q: A company provisions a new, supposedly empty block storage volume from a regional cloud provider. A forensic scan of the volume finds fragments of another customer's database. The provider confirms there was no hypervisor compromise and no misconfiguration by the customer. Which vulnerability BEST explains this?
w: Reallocating storage without sanitizing it exposes the previous tenant's data to the next one. VM escape is breaking out of a guest, VM sprawl is unmanaged growth of VMs, and a side-channel attack infers data from timing or caches rather than leaving it on disk.
h: Somebody else's leftovers on your new plate.

q: A fintech's 40 Kubernetes microservices call each other over plain HTTP. An auditor requires that every call be encrypted and that each service prove its identity to the service it calls, so a compromised pod can't impersonate another. Which approach BEST meets this?
o: A WAF at the cluster's ingress
w: mTLS encrypts each connection and makes both sides present certificates, which proves service identity. Disk encryption protects data at rest, the ingress WAF never sees internal calls, and tokenizing fields neither encrypts the channel nor authenticates services.
h: Both sides show ID, and the line is encrypted.

q: EDR shows no files written to disk. What technique does this sequence show?
c:
parent=WINWORD.EXE child=powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...
powershell.exe -> OpenProcess(explorer.exe, PROCESS_VM_WRITE|PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD)
powershell.exe -> VirtualAllocEx(explorer.exe, 0x3000, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)
powershell.exe -> CreateRemoteThread(explorer.exe)
w: Code is deliberately written into another process's memory with legitimate APIs and run there — for stealth, not new privileges.
h: A hermit crab moving into a shell everyone already trusts.

q: Each regional office sets its own security policies, chooses its own tools, and controls its own budget; HQ only gets quarterly reports. Auditors find inconsistent controls. Which structure is this?
w: Inconsistent controls across units is the signature weakness of decentralized governance.
h: Every location has its own chef — great local food, but the burgers taste different everywhere.

q: Before awarding a contract, a utility asks bidders where their circuit boards and firmware come from and checks those sub-suppliers against restricted-entity lists. What activity is this?
w: Looking at the vendor's own suppliers and component origins is supply chain analysis; right-to-audit is a post-signing contract term.
h: Ask where the caterer buys their meat before you hire them.

q: Two hospitals form a joint venture and sign a document covering how revenue and costs are split, each partner's responsibilities, and data protection duties. Which agreement?
w: Partners splitting revenue in a joint venture is a business partners agreement; an MSA is a customer buying from a vendor.
h: MSA = landlord and tenant. BPA = co-owners of the building.

q: A company signs a three-year umbrella contract with a consultancy setting payment terms and liability, then signs a separate document for each project with deliverables and timelines. What is the per-project document?
w: The umbrella is the MSA; each project's deliverables live in a statement of work.
h: MSA is the umbrella; SOWs are the people standing under it.

q: Customer personal data is spread across a CRM, a marketing platform, ticket attachments, and analysts' spreadsheets, and no one can confirm everywhere it's stored. What should be built FIRST?
w: "Where is it stored?" is answered by the inventory; everything else builds on it.
h: You can't clean the house if you don't know which rooms you own.

q: An EU customer submits a valid erasure request to an online retailer. The retailer holds her marketing preferences, her support chat transcripts, and invoices that tax law requires it to keep for seven years. What is the BEST response?
o: Erase the rest; keep invoices only for the tax duty
Deny the request because some of the data must be kept
Anonymize the invoices and delete everything else
Delete all of it, including the invoices
w: Erasure covers data with no legal basis to keep, while records that a law requires are retained only for that purpose. A legal duty doesn't justify refusing the whole request, anonymizing or deleting the invoices breaks the tax obligation.
h: Erase what you can; keep only what the law makes you keep.

q: A small windowless server room has constant cooling airflow and a thin wall next to a busy hallway. Which motion sensor BEST detects a person after hours with few false alarms?
w: Airflow rules out ultrasonic, the thin wall rules out microwave, and a pressure mat covers one spot.
h: Read the environment clues as eliminators — what's left is the answer.

q: A candidate starts a 90-minute, 90-item practice exam. The first five items are long PBQs, and in her last attempt she spent 40 minutes on them and ran out of time with nine questions unanswered. What is the BEST approach this time?
o: Flag the PBQs, do the multiple choice, then return with time left
Finish each PBQ completely before moving to the next question
Skip the PBQs entirely because they are worth the same as one question
Spend two to three minutes on each multiple-choice item to avoid errors
w: Banking the quicker points first protects against running out of time, and PBQs can still earn partial credit later. Finishing PBQs first repeats last time's problem, PBQs are usually worth more than one multiple-choice item, and three minutes per question would exceed the time limit.
h: Collect the quick points first, then return to the long ones.
